newsitem.title: UK: Oil steady as refinery profits balance Iraq sales.
newsitem.headline: Oil steady as refinery profits balance Iraq sales.

text.p: Oil prices were broadly steady on Monday after a sharp fall last week as buoyant refinery margins provided solid underlying demand to soak up the first Iraqi exports since May.

Iraqi Oil Minister Amir Muhammed Rasheed said exports should restart within two days under the terms of the United Nations oil-for-food deal implemented last December and extended for six months in June.

Bellwether Brent blend crude futures on London's International Petroleum Exchange ended the day up 10 cents at $18.58 a barrel, drawing breath after a 42-cent slide on Friday prompted by the prospect of Iraq's first sales since late May.
Baghdad suspended exports in late May pending U.N. approval of a revised aid distribution plan and now has less than a month to reach the deal's $1 billion interim target set for September 5.

Exports of Iraqi crude from the Gulf terminal of Mina al-Bakr and the Turkish port of Ceyhan will run at about 1.5 million barrels per day (bpd) in August, the highest level since the 1991 Gulf War and more than double the average for the first six months of the U.N. deal.
The deal allows Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil, including pipeline fees, over six months in exchange for food and medicine.

Brokers said expectations of Iraq's return to world markets and the massive crude supply increase that implies was reflected in last week's price fall and that a period of consolidation could be expected.
Prompt demand for refined products like gasoline, and projections of tighter supply of middle distillates like heating oil were providing good support to crude prices, analysts said.
And with growth in product demand for 1997-1998 expected to exceed the increase in refining capacity by the biggest margin for several years, the squeeze on product supply is expected to continue.
"Inventories of gasoline normalised for demand are well below the levels of a year ago," said analysts at Morgan Stanley Dean Witter in a report.
"While absolute inventories of distillate remain high, maximisation of gasoline output should continue in coming weeks, given current margins.
"With the Atlantic Basin short distillate on an annual basis, inventories should be drawn below year ago levels as the heating season unfolds, assuming normal weather," they said.
Margins for a typical complex refinery in Rotterdam averaged $2.84 a barrel last week, more than $1 more than the previous week and the highest level for at least 10 months.
